For dsers:
The first half of the course (before midterm 1) are basically just DSE CORE MATH stats and probi: tree diagram (eg. there are 8 red balls and 5 blue balls in the bag, blablabla...)
Overall not a big disaster as long as you pay attention in class and revise the example questions given during class and on ppt.

But the second part (after quiz 1) is pretty hard, speaking as someone who didn't take M1/M2. There are a lot of new concepts that needed to be studied.

But overall the syllabus of this course is very well-organised and well-planned. The ppt made by Lucy is also very self-learning friendly and easy to follow. Just throw all the ppt into AI, ask AI to explain the concepts to you, then that will be alright
sections.teaching:

She also gave us 10 mins break after teaching for 40 minutes. During the break, students are welcome to ask questions.

sections.content: I believe that ISOM2500 can sometimes be a very tricky subject to learn. More often than not, the quizzes and final felt more like a reading comprehension test than a quantitative test. Where sometimes the worded problems took a long time to read and understand (which could have been a personal problem), you are not only expected to know how to calculate certain results but also understand the metholdogies and logical reasing behind why we calculate this way.
sections.teaching: I personally believe that our profressor was the best ISOM2500 professor in terms of teaching. She has very well structured canvas site, and her powerpoints are simple to understand and learn. Also, she actually does share some practice questions for the quizzes and exams which is very generous. I often found her in class examples to be intuitive and interesting.
sections.grading: While profressors often say that the course won't be curved, so far that hasn't been exactly true in my personal experience. So while I was particularly worried on my perfomance, my final grade didn't turn out as bad as I thought thanks to the professor curving our grades after the finals since the mean was not very high. So as long as you are around the mean, this course can be very forgiving often ending on a B/B+ range. The only downside is that most of the grade is highly dependant on 2 quizzes and 1 final which, can be very stressing and sometimes a small error can be costly.
sections.workload: The workload for the this particular class and professor was very light, while attendance is not exactly mandatory, we needed to complete 5 five in class assignments to get 20% of our grade, which were only graded in terms of completion. The remaining 80% was weighted on the quizzes and final. These in-class assignments are not random and the professor does share when we are expected to come to class and complete them.

sections.content: This course covers the basics of probability and statistics. Topics include probability, random variables, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and simple linear regression. The first half of the course is relatively straightforward if you keep up with the lectures. The later topics, especially hypothesis testing and regression, require a bit more understanding and are more conceptually challenging. Overall, I think the course provides a solid introduction to statistics and is useful for students without much prior background.
sections.teaching: I think Jason teaches quite well. He has a slight Hong Kong accent, but it is easy to understand. The explanations are clear, and he does a good job introducing new concepts step by step. The pace can feel a little slow at times, but it helps students build a strong understanding of the material. I found the lectures helpful and rarely felt lost during class.
sections.grading:
The course consists of online assignments (20%), two quizzes (40%), and a final exam (40%). The assignments are weekly Canvas quizzes, and only the best 7 out of 10 count toward the final grade. The assignments are straightforward if you review the lecture materials carefully. For reference, the mean and standard deviation were 14.9 and 3.8 for Quiz 1, and 11.1 and 3.3 for Quiz 2. The final exam is noticeably harder and requires a deeper understanding of the material, especially the later topics. The final exam mean was 18.4 out of 40 with a standard deviation of 5.2. The grading feels fair overall. I got full marks on the assignments, 21/22 and 17/20 on the two quizzes, and 28/40 on the final exam. Even though I did poorly on the final, I still finished with an A grade.
Notice that this course will be assessed using criterion-referencing and grades will not be assigned using a curve.
sections.workload: The workload is quite manageable. The weekly assignments do not take much time, and they are a good way to review the material. The pressure before the two quizzes is also fairly low because the content is limited and predictable. Most of the workload comes near the end of the semester when hypothesis testing and regression are introduced. These topics require more careful study before the final exam. Other than that, this is one of the lighter quantitative courses I have taken.

sections.content: The course is mainly about basic statistics, but the exam questions are not always straightforward. A lot of questions after quiz 1 require understanding the meaning behind the formula(aka play with wording(very tedious) ). The regression part also includes concepts like R², residuals(but no residuals analysis in this semester), extrapolation, and transformations, so it is important to understand the logic (aka problem set analysis) rather than just memorize calculations. And many content(uniform distribution, chi square, two-sample hypothesis test etc) are skipped, so if you can please consider to take math2411 instead, as final exam is more like applied Regression Analysis.
sections.teaching: The instructor explains the course in a manageable(or trivial) way, and the lecture recordings on Canvas maybe helpful for review. But some topics may feel simple in lecture but become trickier in questions, so prioritize doing problem set or practice question instead of analysing the powerpoint.
sections.grading: The grading is quite fair and generous. There was no midterm, and the grade was based on participation/in-class work, two quizzes( so is 2 midterm?), and the final exam. My scores were 2X/22 on Quiz 1, 13/20 on Quiz 2, 3X/40 on the final, with full participation, and I received A+. So even if one quiz is not perfect, it is still possible to do very well if you keep up with the course and do the participation work.
sections.workload: The workload is not too heavy compared with many other courses. There are not many major assessments, but the questions can be tricky because they often ask about interpretation, assumptions, and choosing the correct conclusion. I would recommend doing the practice problems carefully(btw math2411 problem sets are not useful for this course after quiz/mt 1).

The final is non-cumulative, with 45 MCQs, but is way harder than the midterm. You can have 2 A4 cheat sheets (front and back). The grading is very fair for this course – I would say it gives you a chance to get a high grade even if you do not score high in the final.

sections.content:
Referring to my notes, topics covered include (in ascending order):
**Acquired knowledge prior to university education

Descriptive statistics
-Types of variables
**Presentation methods using graphs

Summary statistics
**SAMPLE mean, median, variance
**Range, IQR, quartiles
-Outliers

Shape of a distribution
**Mode
-Names for different numbers of mode
-Symmetry VS Skew distribution

Conditional probability
**Find P(A|B)
-Contingency/Joint probability table
-Relationship between joint, disjoint, dependent and independent variables
-Bayes' rule

Discrete random variables
**Expected value
-POPULATION mean, variance, SD
-Change in expected value, SD and variance of population data when all data + Constant/x Constant

Bernoulli process & Binomial model
-Sequence of 0 and 1: Success or failure
-Expected value, variance and SD of Binomial model
**Binomial coefficient (nCk)

Association between variables
-Covariance
-Correlation
-Relationship between dependent, independent, correlated and uncorrelated

----- where things get more difficult -----

Sampling distributions
-When to use sample/population statistics
-Difference between sample variance and population variance
-Law of Large Numbers (LLM)
-Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
**Normal distribution
-Z-score of a data by transferring any normal distribution to standard normal distribution
-How to read z-table

Confidence interval (CI)
-Formula/Length of CI
-Margin of error of CI
-CI for probabilities (linkage to Bernoulli process)
-T-tables for data with small n

Hypothesis testing
-Null (Ho) VS Alternative (Ha) hypothesis
-Process of Hypothesis testing
**Type I and Type II error
-Significance level α
-P-value

----- Boss -----

Linear regression (LR)
-Independent/Dependent variable
-β₀, β₁ and Ordinary Least Square (OLS)
-SSE, SST
-R-squared
-Error (ε) in LR
-CI and Hypothesis testing for β₁
-Prediction interval (PI)

A fun course (except LR) but requires strong logical sense.
sections.teaching:
Carsten's teaching is decent. He will answer questions after class so that you actually understand the concepts. I originally would give a B but considering the massive time taken from HW assignments, I will rate a B-.

Overall, the content is not difficult. Only a small portion of the material overlaps with M1 syllabus (Conditional probability, CLT), so don't worry even if you did not study M1 before. However, topic 2,3,4 and 5 are deeply intertwined. For example, you will learn z-distribution and t-distribution in topic 2,3 and they will be used in topic 4 hypothesis testing; then you are required to use hypothesis testing in topic 5 on simple linear regression. So please make sure that you understand the content thoroughly, otherwise the difficulty of the course will increase exponentially.
sections.teaching: Xinyu is a good lecturer. She is eager to answer students' questions patiently and in depth. I still remember that once I asked her a conceptual question after class. And she explained it both in a mathematical way (multivariable differentiation) and in a statistical way. Though I have not learnt multivariable differentiation yet, I could still feel her passion for teaching and her desire to help students. Besides talking to her after class, you can also send her an email. She usually replies to you within 1 hour. Another highlight of Xinyu is no doubt her lecture materials. The PowerPoints are extremely detailed, with many examples (probably 10-20 for one topic) and clearly written (most concepts are presented in bullet points or short sentences, not wordy at all). Lastly, Xinyu provides plenty of exercises for your practice.
sections.grading:
Grading is lenient; I thought I would get a B+, but eventually I got an A.

Total grade consists of the following parts:
1. Homework assignments (20%)
You will be asked to finish 5 in-class assignments throughout the course. They are graded by participation i.e. even if you get 1 mark in the assignment, you will rececive full marks automatically. Xinyu will even remind you one lesson before each in-class assignment. All you need to do is just attend the lesson and finish the assignment before the lesson ends.
2. Mid-term exam (25%)
3. Final exam (55%)

My grade:
Homework: full marks
Mid-term: 23/24
Final: 27/45
Total: 77.0% A

Statistics for the midterm (full mark 24)
mean:16.6 mode:15 median:17 max:24 min:6 s.d.: 4.33
No statistics for the final

I have to be honest that the midterm is tricky. From the data, you can observe that the s.d. is quite small compared to s.d. in other courses (usually above 10), indicating that scores are tightly clustered around 16-17. However, this is reasonable because the time was too short, I could barely finish all the questions a few minutes before the end of exam. As for the final, it was EXTREMELY DIFFICULT. I am quite a diligent student and I spend most of my time in ISOM2500, I even finished all the exercises provided by Xinyu. However, I was still confused when I was taking the final exam. I felt like all my hard work was useless, even though I understood every page in the lecture notes, final exam questions appeared completely different. As mentioned above, I got only 27/45, just 60%, but still got an A ultimately. You can see how difficult the exam was. Therefore, as my personal advice, please pay attention in class if you aim for an A range, make sure you complete all the optional exercises and quizzes. Even if you feel like you performed poorly after the final exam, don't worry, it's normal, and I believe all your hard work will be reflected in your grade.
sections.workload: Compared with other lecturers, you do not need to worry about assignments in Xinyu's course. Therefore, this course should have minimal workload. However, this is double-edged because all your classmates will get full marks on their assignments and your final grade will depend solely on your midterm and final exams. Unless you are confident about taking exams, you should carefully consider whether you take Xinyu's lecture. As a last reminder, workload may be large for those who aim for an A range because you really need to spend a lot of time on understanding the material.

sections.content:
Topic 1 graphical tools: just some example of basic things to show stats
Topic 2 descriptive statistics: basics like mean mode median variance… and value at risk, mostly high school content
Topic 3 Association and dependence: covariance, correlation, Chi-squared statistic, Cramer’s V to understand strength of association, more maths is done here
Topic 4 Probability and conditional probability: basic probability, learned in high school
Topic 5 discrete random variables: sharp ratio, Bernoulli distribution, binomial distribution, this topic is more complicated use of variance and expected value and probability
Topic 6 continuous random variables: more understanding to normal distribution, value at risk and t-distribution, you will use a lot of Excel here
Topic 7 sampling distribution: more understanding to sample vs population, proportion, quite important because you need to recall these later
Topic 8 interval estimation: confidence interval, not hard to understand but more calculation is done and Excel used here
Topic 9 hypothesis testing: one-side test vs two-side test, z-statistic, statistic test for proportion, pay more attention to this topic, don’t mix up things, nearly all Excel formulas you learnt from previous lessons are used
Topic 10 simple linear regression: assumptions for linear regression, interpretation and diagnosis

2 labs about Excel, you need Excel for whole course even in final.
When you did enough practicing in maths. You find things easier.

Carsten's pronounciation is acceptable but not exceptionally clear and he tends to use lengthy sentences to explain concepts. This makes his lesson a bit hard to concentrate.

Prof's class slides is pretty interesting tho, he types on every sentence he is going to say in class as bullet sentences (not paragraphs) to present a logical thinking process to us.(slides sample below) With such slides, you'll have to highlight the keywords and locate the formulas scattered across pages yourself, so I don't recommend only reviewing everything before exams.

I like that he opens up discussion forrums on Canvas for us to post questions. This eliminated the trouble of writing a whole formal email and the information can be accessed by everyone.

I don't like the fact that he is late for 5-15mins in nearly every class and only do the job upload the slides to Canvas right before the lesson starts.
I think it is a waste of time even though he mangaed to keep his teaching on schedule.

Regarding to the poor logistics. The second Quiz delayed for over half an hour cuz the TA and Prof had to place the papers one by one.(You should've done that before the lesson starts!) I suppose the TA Kenrick should be familiar with such tasks but seemed not.
In Prof's DEFENSE, he did mention that this is the first teaching semester at UST and he only teaches every other semester, so I hope he does better later on.

TA Kenrick, he was patient when answering our questions in paper checking sessions. From my observation his English is not good enough to answer questions in person so you should email him or ask Prof directly.

One thing I would like to complain about is that the practice quizzes he posted on Canvas are not really tailor-made for our final exam as some questions of the practice quizzes are out of syllabus and some wordings can’t match with what he taught in class since the practice quizzes were not made by him! The final exam is so complicated and completing all the homework and practice quizzes didn’t help me gain high marks in the final as his homework focuses more on teaching concepts than exam preparations.

For the TA Kenrick, he is also a good teacher who teaches with heart. You can see him at the paper checking sessions and you can ask him to explain the quiz questions that you don’t understand and of course any other questions related to the course content. He is able to explain clearly and in detail.

For topics taught before mid-term, they are the easiest things I have ever come across in Year 1.  However, things started to change after mid-term, when normal distribution was introduced.  All post-mid-term topics tie closely to normal distribution, and once you master test statistics, they become straightforward, EXCEPT FOR LINEAR REGRESSION.  It is critical for your grade, as it integrates everything learnt in the course. You must be able to distinguish between different variables, particularly the 4 standard deviations (Sx, Sy, Sβ1, S), where people often mix them up.

btw I didn't take M1 or M2 in DSE

sections.teaching:
Carsten is a new professor with decent English. I personally find it easy to catch up with his teaching. He does not count attendance and lecture videos are provided. Do watch them if concepts are unclear.

He would also assign some questions to us during class. He will walk around and make sure most, if not all students know how to do before he move on. Feel free to ask him any questions and he is very willing to answer.

His slides are also clear and useful. However, do note that Carsten uses terms that other profs may not use (e.g. he uses "OLS" while other prof uses "LSE".). So it might take you some time to get use to it as well as it might be confusing during exams as other profs ask questions using other terms.
sections.grading:
Carsten is very lenient in terms of grading.

For quizzes, we are not allowed to bring any calculators and he tends to ask conceptual questions rather than mathematical questions. So, I think it's trickier than the exams.

Mid term is quite easy. Just make sure you answer all the questions and do not skip any question like me. I literally thought there was only 20 MC questions during the exam, but turns out it's 23.

Final is hard. Keep in mind that the time is limited and allocate your time wisely.

Marks:
Quiz 1(10%): 15/20 (Median 16/20)
Quiz 2(10%): 12/20 (Median 12/20, LQ 10/20, UQ 14/20)
Mid term(30%): 20/23 (Median 17/20, LQ 14/23, UQ 19/23)
Final(50%): 24/40 (Not revealed)

Final Grade: A-
sections.workload:
You got to do homework every week and if you miss more than 2 homework, Carsten will deduct 20% of your quiz score.

Note that all homework are individual assignment, unlike group projects in other sessions.

Some might find it much workload, but I personally thought that it's a good way to facilitate your study. Just take it as a revision every week and you will be fine.

sections.content:
1. Types of data (numerical, categorical, histogram, DATA SECURITY AND PRIVACY, standard deviation, central value, skewness, IQR, box plot)
2. Venn Diagram, Probability (sample space, independence, bayes' rule, random variables, expected values, variance)
3. Probability distribution (binomial distribution)
4. Normal distribution (standard normal curve, standardization)
5. Sampling distribution (central limit theorem)
6. Statistical Estimation (confidence interval estimators, width, small sample estimation of mean, degree of freedom)
7. Hypothesis testing (type I and II error, alpha and beta, critical value, p-value, test statistic, paired difference test)
8. Correlation and linear regression (r, rho, regression analysis, simple regression model, lest square estimation, prediction interval, R^2)

sections.content:
Descriptive statistics→Probability, random variables→Inferential statistics including simple linear regression.
I attached an overview of this course summarized by Mr. Ho, you can refer to it. I think it summarizes quite well.
Quite boring. Since this is Business Statistics, everything is put under some business context(which I think is really unnecessary), like how to predict a cost, how to assess a product, something. If you love business, maybe you'll find it interesting. But I hate business so I thought it dull. They don't provide any proof of those techniques and formulas, not even much explanation on why it looks like that. They will just tell you what that is and how to use it. If you are curious about why, see "Behind the Math" session in the recommended textbook.
Much content is omitted, lowering the workload but you'll learn less in the meantime.
There are two Excel labs, a calculator workshop(去的都是nds, 我猜是因为只有高考不能用计算器，不会使，而其他人早已在中学学过), not mandatory. The content in those is not included in tests, but some skills will help in asm, and maybe in future work?
Btw, the textbook is available in our liba. Here's the link
https://julac-hkust.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/discovery/search?vid=852JULAC_HKUST:HKUST&tab=Everything&search_scope=HKUST_catalog_primo&query=any,contains,Statistics%20for%20Business%20Decision%20Making%20and%20Analysis
sections.teaching:
Mr. Ho is a nice person, he smiled and said thank you when he collected my final paper, making me feel better after the torture of statistics. ^_^ He is willing to answer my questions even if they are quite stupid.
What needs noting is that he enjoys reframing the knowledge in the textbook with colorful PPT. I guess he did so to better adjust to the omitted syllabus. As a result, hardly can you predict what he’s going to introduce next lecture, especially since he won’t unlock the PPT until he delivers the lecture. =_= I mentioned this problem in SFQ in the hope that he could accept my suggestion to unlock it in advance. We will see.
Anyway, his PPT was useful, you can learn well by following his lectures and PPT, even if you don’t read the textbook. Actually, from my personal experience, reading the textbook will make you struggle with adopting two different frameworks at the same time. But it helps to understand. So, you can trade off between.
TA was Alex. He was the best TA I met and I guess no one will be better during the rest of 4 years. Many TAs are too busy to give you a f***, but Alex accompanied us every lecture, answered our questions, and conducted computer labs.
*I totally understand why TAs are so busy and not mean to blame. I just want to emphasize good TAs like Alex are so rare. Thanks should be given to them.
很多TA没空鸟本科生，但是Alex会鸟我们，他是个大好人
sections.grading:
You just need to remember and be skilled in all techniques(成为熟练工) to get a good grade. ╮(╯_╰)╭ Nevertheless, on top of proficiency, a good grasp of concepts can help you outperform. There are some questions that will test your understanding of concepts in the final. But personally speaking, skills play a bigger role in your grade.
Here are the grading compositions. Also, I took some screenshots of the mark distributions and attached them below.
Attendance(5%) Mr. Ho posts online quizzes randomly at any time in his lectures. Finish them in order to get attendance. But you can actually do them out of class hhh. One of my friends did it in Shenzhen.
Group Assignment×2(7.5%each) Disaster for those who don't have high school classmates, don't social much, didn't even in pmp of MSSSUG like me. How are you supposed to find group mates when you are in this uni for only 2 weeks? Thankfully the group mates I randomly group up with are good persons. If yours not you can actually report to prof.
Group asms include some computation problems, some conceptual problems, and some asking you for a graph generated by Excel. In fact, you can do them all alone, but as far as I know, that will turn out with low accuracy. So still, better check answers with your group mates.
Midterm(30%) 20 super easy multiple-choice. Just be really careful to get full marks. 2 cheat sheets are allowed.
After the midterm, the difficulty has rocketed. I found it harder to understand those concepts and techniques. Definitely you need more attention to figure out all the things, but I guess remembering them (or simpler, noting them on your cheat sheets) might be just enough to help you through exams, despite not much chance to excel.
Final(50%) 45 quite hard multiple-choice. Same with the midterm, you can have 2 pieces of cheat sheet. Mr. Ho told us to be psychologically prepared for the final since it would be harder and indeed it was. The time was tight, that’s why I said you need to be skilled in all techniques. Mr. Ho posts many exercises on Canvas, they are similar to exams. I suggest you practice them before exams so that you can save time from looking up things in cheat sheets. Literally, you won’t have much time to waste appreciating your cheat sheets during exams.

Course outline (40%): A-
Quality of course material (60%): C-

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

 The course content is nearly the same as previous years. You can check out the document.

 Difficulty:
Contents before quiz 1: 3/10
Contents from quiz 1 to quiz 2: 5.5/10
Contents from quiz 2 to final exam: 9/10

 Before hypothesis testing, most of the topics are covered in DSE M1, so you would have a great advantage if you have studied M1.

 However, the content suddenly becomes very hard when getting into hypothesis testing and simple regression.

 The content does NOT contain calculus, proofs and some important statistical concepts like Poisson distribution, geometric distribution and statistical inferences. Therefore, this course is not as rigorous as MATH 2411/3423 but serves as a general statistics course.

 Professor James's PPTs are quite messy, so you may need to reorganize what he says in the PPTs by making your summary notes.

 One good thing is that his examples are highly related to business cases and models, like the CAPM model in simple regression.

 There are two optional online lab tutorials for you to attend. TA mainly focuses on how to use Excel to solve calculation problems in assignments.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Professor James

 Jamaica professor

 The teaching quality is below average compared to other professors I have met before.

 He always claims that he would simplify things for our understanding. Also, he tries to relate different concepts to business, which is coherent with one of the aims of this course (but sometimes talks too much). That’s good.

 However, He usually tells some jokes in class (often I think they are not funny and just annoying) and laughs, and he seems to like teaching international students more than local students :) His hand-written supplementary notes during class are not very helpful for us to understand the concepts, plus his teaching schedule in each lesson is often messy, making me confused usually. Also, he usually makes things more complicated than they should be (which contradicts his claim about simplicity in teaching).

 Sometimes he skip a whole example or even a whole PPT and tell us to read by ourselves :)

 Furthermore, there is 10% of attendance scores. It is supposed that we should attend at least 18 out of 26 lectures, but he never takes attendance, so I still don’t know how to grade this part.

 He also don't like students leaving the lecture theatre early, especially when you are not an international student :)), so you should either attend the whole lecture or skip the lecture and watch the lecture recording.

2. TA

 She does an OK job on teaching the required EXCEL skills in the lab sessions.

 Read the following part below. This shows how low the quality of her and professor as a responsible TA and professor!!!

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

 The most terrible thing in this course is the set up of questions in quiz 2! The TA set up 3 out of 10 MCQs WRONGLY so nearly everyone get full marks on these questions. More importantly, when I point out the mistakes via email, professor James at first simply give some unreasonable and irrelevant explanations to argue that the set up of these questions are correct. I explain to him again via email and he again give shitty 1 line explanation to defend himself. Until I show the mathematical steps and graph plotted using Desmos (one question is about transformation of normal distribution curve), he finally realize the mistakes and tell the TA to correct the students' marks.

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

 Nevertheless, it is good for allowing us to use excel in the exam as we can learn the skills needed when we handle statistics in the real world (You won't use the tables anymore in the workplace right?).

 Also, he is quite nice and sometimes give you some hints about what would be tested in the quizzes and final exam during lectures.

 Furthermore, he is kind and welcomes your help (only when he takes care your questions or you are an international student :D)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

I believe the reason why his teaching quality is low in this course is because he is the chair professor of ISOM department. He may use the same way that he teaches postgraduate students to teach undergraduate students, which is not appropriate.

sections.content:
The content is not useful. Not as rigorous as a math/stat course, but also not very practical for a sbm course. Basically 兩頭唔到岸
(Update: More applications will actually be covered in 2600)

Before midterm:
Basic statistics concepts, summary statistics (mean mode median), probability, binomial distribution
Extremely easy. For DSE students, it's like 30% difficulty of probability questions in core maths (but remember to study more about Bayes theorem)

After midterm:
Normal distribution, sampling distribution, confidence interval, hypothesis testing, linear regression and regression analysis
Everything except regression analysis is rather abstract to understand, but manageable if you take some time to study.
Regression analysis, however, is another world. In the exam they let us comprehend a whole regression table but they've never taught how to interpret it in class.

45 questions in the final exam, about 15 questions about regression analysis are practically impossible to do, and some other conceptional questions are confusing af as well.
sections.teaching:
Teaches everything clearly and tries to let you understand the concept, easy to follow without statistics/M1 background.
His pet phrases are "this is extremely important" and "we ask our phd candidates this question…" etc.

However the last few lectures were disastrous. He was teaching in light speed and we couldn't follow anything he said, which made one of the reasons why we couldn't understand regression analysis.
Bro should just learn some time management, don't waste your time on the first few easy chapters.

Also, it's worth mentioning that the TA wasn't doing her job. There were many typos in the assignments and the questions are often unclear. For each assignment we had to email her to ask 4-5 questions for her to clarify.

sections.workload:
The workload is quite light, only 3 group assignment in total, each takes around 2 hours if you want to finish it individually.

The only drawback may be the two quizzes. The first quiz is held on early March and the second quiz is held on early April, so they are likely to be your first and last tests you need to take in the midterm period.

sections.content: It starts out easy (e.g. mean, median, mode, how to conduct surveys etc) and by the end it's topics that are not too difficult but require a lot of brain power to understand (e.g. linear regression). But it's hard to comment on the content because it's just standard stuff for any beginner statistics class.
sections.teaching: Jason's accent is classic HK accent. He's really boring and uses too many symbols and abbreviations in his powerpoints. However I appreciate how many examples he uses in his slides, because I can self-learn the content after class in case I fall asleep. He's also very petty about taking attendance and making sure that people don't sign in for others. And he sometimes forgets to pass the attendance sheet around and we all have to stay after class to sign in and risk being late for our next class because of his mistake.
sections.grading: Most of the grade is from the mid term and final exam, so make sure to study hard. They were noncumulative so if you try hard enough you should do ok. We also had mini quizzes every week that were 3% each (no calculations, all theory and T/F questions.) that force you to come to class. But he is lenient about attendance (somewhat), because you only need to be present for 2/3 of the semester.
sections.workload: The workload is quite light. There are no weekly assignments, but that just means that your grade is mostly from your mid-term and final exam.

The quizzes, exam, and homework for Lucy's class are computational-oriented, which is not that hard, to be honest. You may come across some tricky questions but most can be solved using the formulae taught in lessons. Seemingly the grading for Lucy's class will be good. But not really. Because most of the students are able to complete all the tasks without really understanding the content, the mark distribution of all the tasks is extremely left-skewed. If you are a careful person that can minimize the number of stupid mistakes during exams, Lucy is your best choice for ISOM 2500.

There were also two quizzes, covering 2-3 chapters each. The quizzes were of acceptable difficulty, and there was a flexible time limit.

sections.content: If you have done IB HL applications and interpretations or A level Mathematics Stats option, the content should be relatively straight forward as it covers most of the fundamental statistical concepts such as normal, binomial distribution, descriptive stats, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals (this was heavily emphasized in the final exam). The last topic, being the simple regression model is slightly new so you may need more time to digest the concept.

sections.workload:
There are around 20-25 pieces of homework which has to do with calculations and excel spreadsheet work and Kohei usually takes the best 6 so it is strongly encouraged that you max out the first 6 pieces of homework as they are relatively the easiest. After that, it just comes down to preparation for the midterms and finals.

If you have not studied stats before, the course may be challenging as there are some advanced concepts towards the end, especially after the mid terms (Don't be fooled by the level of difficulty of the first midterm quiz!).

Although, if you have prior stats knowledge, e.g. IB SL analysis and approaches, assuming that you have studied normal distribution in the past, you may be familiar with concepts up to the midterm but towards the finals the concepts will be slightly different and a bit more in depth such as T test, Z test, hypothesis testing, regression analysis.

If you have taken more advanced stats courses in High school ie A level further math stats, IB HL applications, AP stats, etc.. there should be around an 80-90% course overlap so therefore, most of the course content should be relatively straightforward. However, bear in mind that towards the end the inferential statistics gets rather interesting and sophisticated.

sections.teaching:
Professor Kawaguchi is a super nice prof who would answer your questions and explain the concepts until you understand. You can easily reach him/Stacey through the Slack workspace he opened for the class. His approachable and humble character makes the class atmosphere lively!
He gave mock mid-terms and finals for us to practice the MCQs. Those exercise tests have explanations and answers so make sure you go through them at least once before the tests! (some MCQs (roughly 3-4 per test) are copied from the mock test )
One thing to note is that Professor Kawaguchi's Japanese accent was quite strong, it could take about 3-4 lessons to have a better grasp of what he is saying... so make sure you know some Japanese (hiragana lol) and note the way how he pronounces some common words to help yourself follow his useful and chill teaching. For example...

Putting stress on the second syllable:
paTURN -> pattern
moDALE -> model

'k' -> 'c'
suKAra -> scalar

'sym'/'s' -> 'shi'
shimbol -> symbol
shimmatric -> symmetric
shingulu -> single

'age' -> 'ji'
pAsentaji -> percentage  

'r' -> 'l'
rike -> like
onrine -> online
raptop -> laptop
recture -> lecture
raBEL -> level

'f' -> 'v' and 'th'
falue -> value
fariable -> variable
freshold -> threshold

Typical ones:
klum -> column
huust -> host
ofun -> often
je-score -> z-score
pikus -> peaks
Gugu -> Google
bugu -> bag
wrist -> list
aahfarege -> average

I don't mean to tease Professor Kawaguchi's accent. I only hope to list some examples here to illustrate there were patterns in his pronunciation. After taking some time to understand, you would find his lectures even more enjoyable. I really like his structured and rich teaching!

sections.content:
Interesting Statistics:
Syllabus:
- Data and variation.
- Time series data.
- Transform data.
- Probability and its rules.
- Tools for organizing probability.
- Probability models.
- Variance and volatility of investments.
- Association and dependence.
- Covariance and portfolio.
- Normal probability distribution.
- Sampling.
- Sampling distributions.
- Standard errors and confidence intervals.
- Statistical hypothesis testing.
- Fitting equation to data.
- The simple regression model. ( Everything learned before is preparing you to delve into this course's most important part!! Regression is used to do forecasting!)
- Inference about SRM
- Introduction to multiple regression.
sections.teaching: Although some may feel difficult to adapt to Prof Du's accent, it is not that bad, you just need to pay more attention in class. Really cares about his teaching quality. heard him sigh after class, worrying if the students really understand the topic. Friendly, chats with students and tries his best to satisfy their wants.
sections.grading: Nice grades, Prof Du tries his best to give A to students. Just perform well in 2 mid terms and 1 final, get 1-2SD above mean, you'll end up with an A range.
sections.workload:
The 3 assignments are group work so it's easy to finish them. An hour or two should be enough for each assignment.
Revision for midterms and exams is not very time-consuming so the workload is quite light.

sections.content:
I agree that this syllabus gives students who studied M1 an advantage in terms of workload, as topics such as probability, normal distribution, and confidence intervals, as they have already learned it.
However, the syllabus of the whole course for this Professor is relatively the easiest and shortest when compared to other professors in this semester, as it did not drill deep into more difficult topics such as the Simple Regression Model.
sections.teaching:
Professor Kohei has a very heavy Japanese accent, and it can be difficult to catch his words in face-to-face lessons and even harder in zoom recordings. I think his explanations are quite clear for people with or without M1. His PowerPoint slides are mainly a summary from the book, so you can understand the course content by referring back to the book or search for videos on YouTube. However, sometimes he spent a lot of time talking about the proof of equations and rationale behind it, so his teaching speed is overall rather slow.
He also uses a software called "Slack" to communicate with his students and release course and exam materials. We can reach out to him and TA for any questions easily, which is very convenient.
sections.grading:
The syllabus for each quiz is not too much. All quizzes are said to be cumulative, but in fact, there are not many questions on the tested chapters. For the two quizzes, they are comparatively easy as they are very similar to the sample paper they provided. So, the mean and median for each quiz are very high, and getting one MC wrong can cost you a lot. The final is relatively more difficult, so I would say the score of your finals can make a HUGE difference in terms of your final grade. I suggest getting sources (e.g. question bank) to prepare for exams, as there is a large chance the same question type would appear in the quizzes and exams

sections.content:
In this course, you will learn about the basics of statistics.

These are the main topics:
Association/Dependence, Random Variables, Covariance, Normal Distribution, Sampling Distribution, Confidence Interval, Hypothesis Testing, Simple Linear Regression

The contents become more detailed later on, so make sure you understand the contents taught on the first half before you do not understand them later on.
sections.teaching:
Professor Jason is really passionate about his teaching. He uses a lot of examples in his slides, so even if you do not understand the theory at first, you will after you go through the examples with him.

The slides he gives is very detailed and organized, it really helped me a lot to understand.

If you have any questions, make sure you ask him. He will try his best to answer your question. He is a very kind and a fun person to talk to.
sections.grading:

sections.workload:

sections.content:
If you did IB Math AI HL, this course is very similar (especially the first few topics)!

sections.teaching:
Professor DU, Lilun is really nice and helpful. He is also funny and tries to make lessons interesting and engaging. He always gives us a break in the middle of the class, to ensure we don't burn out.

For one of the "game" lessons, he even gave us M&M candies to visually illustrate one of the probability ideas taught earlier on.

After class or during office hours, you can find him and he's extremely helpful when explaining a concept or answering your questions.

Overall, I really enjoyed his classes.
sections.grading:
Grade Composition:

Attendance: 5% (by iPRS)
Assignments: 15%
Quiz 1: 20%
Quiz 2: 20%
Final Exam: 40%

Prof Lilun Du is smart, as he will randomly take attendance so that students can't "prepare" and only attend lectures on those days. My advice—attend them all.

As for the assignments (3 in total), we were given an option to do them alone or form groups. Either way, they're not too bad as each one only has a few questions (around 6 to 7) and should be manageable if you paid attention in lectures.

Quiz 1, Quiz 2 and Finals are all MC exams, with the quizzes being 20 questions each while the final exam has 40. Quiz 1 and 2 were extremely easy, while finals are a bit more challenging. A one-page A4 cheat sheet is allowed for all these assessments.

I think this course has fair grading.
sections.workload:
I personally think the workload is extremely manageable if you do things in a timely manner and don't keep pushing things to the future. Plus, the first two quizzes (Quiz 1 + Quiz 2) are quite easy and very similar to the practice quiz he hands out for our preparation. He even threw in some exact questions from the practice set in those quizzes!

My advice is—as long as you follow the pace of the lectures and do the recommended work, you'll be fine in this course!

sections.teaching:
Prof. Du is the best professor, period. His accent may be a bit hard to understand when you first hear it, but you'll get used to it in no time. Aside from his accent, his teaching is flawless. He makes his own PowerPoints so you don't need to waste a few hundreds on buying the textbook. His explanations are very clearly and concise. He is even better than some of my high school teachers!

Most importantly, he will upload exercise onto canvas before every exams. You can practice and get an idea of what types of question will appear in the test. He will also hold a tutorial before each exams so you can ask questions if you don't understand the course material.

Swapping to his lecture is one of the best decision I've ever made. He is an angel sent by god to save students.

2nd midterm: Mean 15.7/20 SD 2.8 (highest 20)

I get 20 in the 1st midterm, 19 in the 2nd one and 37 in the final exam. For the 3 assignments and I get an average of 99.33. Attendance is easy marks so I get all 5%. Final score is 95.9 with the highest being 96.9.
Letter grade A+

Here are some tips to get good grade:
1. For both midterms, remember to do the exercises given by Prof. Du. Redo them for a few times to make sure you understand all the content.
2. Review the ppts before exam. Make sure you understand all of the content taught during lecture. Some terms are kind of confusing so be careful when doing revision. For instance, sample and population.
3. Both midterms and the final exam are multiple choice so the overall difficulty is not too high,
4. Assignment is a groupwork so it is easy to get high mark. However, you can choose to not join any group and do it by yourself. There are just 7 or 8 questions per assignment so it's not difficult even if you don't have teammates. Just pay attention to the details in question, as some questions are quite tricky. If you have problems, just ask the TA or the prof. Try to score as high as you can.
5. Prof. Du only take attendance in 5 lectures and he will usually tell you in advance. Easy marks.
6. Although the 2 midterms is really easy(even homework is harder than midterms), the final exam is incredibly difficult. Just doing the exercises is far from enough. You need to have perfect understanding of everything taught in class, especially the part about Regression diagnosis. EVERY DETAIL IS IMPORTANT. EVERY SENTENCE IN THE PPT IS CRUCIAL. Review the lecture recording for at least once.
7. Cheat sheet(A4 size) is allowed in the midterms and final exam. Besides from formula, copying definition of some confusing terms can be helpful too.

It is extremely hard to get A+ as only the top 2~3% can get an A+, which means that only 4~6 students can get A+. I think you need to score around 95 to get an A+.

Getting in A range is not hard though, as the midterms and assignment is easy. Just put in effort and you can get a good grade. Effort always pay off.

Most concepts from Ch.1-8 have been covered in high school subjects such as Mathematics. Starting from Ch.9, there will be a considerable number of equations and formulas introduced, as well as new (and abstract) concepts. Starting from Ch.15, it gets the hardest and the concepts are difficult to understand thoroughly. 1 lesson per chapter on average.

The textbook can be accessed for free online. There is no need to purchase a new one since it is not compulsory.
sections.teaching:
Mr. Kawaguchi has a Japanese accent when teaching but it didn't take us very long to get used to it. Since the keywords are on the PowerPoint, we usually know what he is referring to and talking about.

He will do a review before the mid-term and final exams. There is usually a sample mock paper (not a compulsory assignment) provided the week before, and the lesson before the exam will be used to check it.

Mr. Kawaguchi and the syllabus say that attendance is compulsory but he never actually takes the attendance. I see some people being absent but the attendance rate for his classes is usually high.

We also use a platform called 'Slack workspace' (similar to Discord but we don't use it for calls) for asking questions publicly or anonymously, receiving announcements and slides, exam info, etc. He allows us to ask questions via this platform in lessons.
sections.grading:
Mr. Kawaguchi's exams are all closed-book and no cheat sheets are allowed. More effort may be needed to remember the formulas but his papers are at an acceptable level of difficulty and are relatively easier than other professors.

Absolute grading is used. The following is copied from the syllabus on Canvas.
1. Approximately A range for >= 90, B range for >= 80, and C range for >= 50.
2. Midterm 30%: There are two quizzes. The exams are cumulative, but the first exam mainly tests
Part I (15%) and the second exam mainly tests Part II (15%), respectively. The questions in the exam
include both multiple-choice and discussions. The questions do not ask how to use excel. The exams
are closed-book. I provide mock exams and review in the class. The problems are like the end of chapter problems in the textbook.
3. Final Exam 40%: The exam is cumulative but mainly covers Part III. The questions in the final exam
include both multiple-choice and discussions. The questions do not ask how to use excel. The exams
are closed-book. I provide the mock exam and review in the class. The problems are like the end of
chapter problems in the textbook.
4. Assignments 30%: I assign one exercise per chapter. The main purpose of the assignments is to
assess whether the students understand the concepts and can use excel to solve problems. Each
exercise has 5% point. For each student, I give scores based on the best 6 submissions if you submit more than 6 assignments. The deadline will be 1 week for each exercise.
sections.workload:
There is one assignment for every chapter (19 in total for my semester). Only the 6 assignments with the highest scores will be counted and used to calculate the homework score. The assignments are not compulsory so you can choose not to do them if you already got the full score. The earliest assignments are very simple Excel exercises about making charts and graphs with demonstration videos to follow, so full marks for the 30% assignment score can be easily claimed.

The only shortcoming is that the skills of the earliest assignments (especially Excel-based ones) are not relevant to the course at all.

sections.teaching:
He was very passionate and enthusiastic about what he was teaching, keeping a positive atmosphere. You might not understand the content of each lecture immediately, but rewatching the lectures will definitely help you make more sense of it. He often pulls up his whiteboard for further elaboration on the concepts, the things he mentions on the whiteboard are sometimes extra info beyond what you're required to learn in the course. If you reach out for help, he will definitely help you clarify concepts and explain them to you until you get it!

He also teaches at his own pace, so our class was often a sub-chapter or two behind other classes.
sections.grading:
I think you will get the grade you work for. Although the mean was quite high for both quizzes and the final. Here's the weighting for each component:
Quiz 1 - 20%
Quiz 2 - 20%
Group Assignments - 10%
Final - 40%
Attendance - 10% (don't know how this was calculated since it was never released, I think they do take your attendance though)

CLASS STATISTICS:
Quiz 1: 7.9/10 (SD 1.21)
Quiz 2: 7.6/10 (SD 1.89)
Assignment 1: 11.3/13
Assignment 2: 13.1/14
Assignment 3: 22.8/26
Final: 16/20  (SD 2.67)

Both quizzes and final were open book

Quizes were quite straight forward, pay attention in class and he'll give hints on a few questions he's gonna ask in the quiz!

The final exam wasn't too hard, there was a mixture of calculations and conceptual questions - for these know the purpose of each statistical tool and why it's used in a particular context. The level of difficulty of the final was slightly harder than the quizzes.

Final Grade: A
sections.workload:
The workload wasn't too high, you just need to rewatch all the lectures and take note of + be familiar with all the examples shown in the ppts as those will help you put the concepts into practice. Some questions that came up in the quiz/final were very similar to the ppt examples!

If you want an extra resource to understand the materials, jbstatistics on youtube was very helpful as their videos were concise and had examples!!! The textbook was somewhat useful, but it was quite lengthy so I watched videos instead.

There were also 2 tutorials, attendance wasn't recorded here. Tutorials mainly focused on using excel to solve problems related to the assignments.

sections.teaching:
Lecturer: XIA, Lucy
The best lecturer I have met in UST so far!

Super nice
Super patient when answering questions both in lectures and email. She will try different approaches to explain until you understand it.

High proficiency of spoken English
Her English is pretty close to native (maybe she is native, idk). Totally understandable.

High ability of explaining concept

Perfectly-organized and well-written ppt
the ppts are rich in content and explanation yet simple and clear. You don't need the textbook if you have her ppts

Highly organized and valuable lectures
Opening a new topic, she follows this flow:
1. begins by briefly capturing the whole idea and structure of the topic
2. in-depth explanation of concept
3. clear, step by step answering approach: if you follow her approaches of answering questions, you will get full mark
4. review of the content taught in the last lesson at the beginning of every lectures. It really helps consolidate your understanding and memory of the contents if you follow through the review

Systematic practice resources
The format of the 4 homeworks is the same as the 2 quizzes and final exam. Before each quiz and exam, she uploads a practice quiz or exam. So in total, you could say there are 7 sets of whole paper to practice. If you do all these, check the answers and understand your mistake, you will definitely do well in the quizzes and exam

I regret not filling the official lecturer evaluation at the end of the semester. The tremendous effort of Lucy should be well-promoted and acknowledged. If you enrolled her classes and agreed, please do so!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

TA: Deng, Stacy
Overall very good TA as well

Very nice
She answers your emails very patiently even after many rounds of follow-up questions. She genuinely wants you to understand the materials.

Coherent paper setting and high quality material
She is the one who sets the HWs, quizzes and exam. They are all so coherent in terms of format, which makes them really good for practice.

Good written English but comparatively weak spoken English
When she writes email, her English is good that she is able to explain concepts in a clear manner. But during tutorials where she needs to speak impromptuly, it takes her some time to process her words and the explanation is not good. But the tutorials cover answering approaches that are also covered in Lucy's lectures, so you may attend tutorials only if you find it hard to follow Lucy's lectures or ppts.

sections.content:

2. Things started to get a little more complex when random variables were introduced in the 9/10th lecture. The difficulty of the content increased significantly and you really have to go through the powerpoint slides and attend lectures to grasp the content. Topics that were covered included hypothesis testing, random variables and regression model. If you did not take any statistics course in high school, the second half of the course could be a little challenging for you and much effort must be placed in this course.

You must be extremely attentive to understand what he is teaching. Apart from his spoken English, his teaching isn't too bad. sections.content:
The content is well prepared and the course mainly focuses on the application side of statistics, so need not worry about rigorous maths proof
Syllabus:
- Data and variation.
- Time series data.
- Transform data.
- Probability and its rules.
- Tools for organizing probability.
- Probability models.
- Variance and volatility of investments.
- Association and dependence.
- Covariance and portfolio.
- Normal probability distribution.
- Sampling.
- Sampling distributions.
- Standard errors and confidence intervals.
- Statistical hypothesis testing.
- Fitting equation to data.
- The simple regression model. ( Everything learned before is preparing you to delve into this course's most important part!! Regression is used to do forecasting!)
- Inference about SRM
- Introduction to multiple regression.
sections.teaching: Prof Hu teaches very clearly by explaining the concepts in details. He included some experiment during the class which helped us to understand the concept better.

sections.teaching:
Professor is passionate about the course. He is kind and approachable during and after lectures. Some students complain of his thick accent, but you’ll get used to it after 3 or so lectures, and the accent doesn’t affect the content he teaches.

T.A. was responsive to e-mails so if you have any queries, just keep bothering the T.A. especially during preparation for finals (lower mean of the finals shows its increased difficulty compared to the two quizzes).

I also tried contacting the professor through e-mail, but he would take longer to respond.
sections.grading:
With regards to the university grading scheme, the grading is fair. It is, after all, a statistics course that teaches you about the normal distribution curve lol. However, my largest complaint is that the course tests your consistency (like how careless) more than your understanding of the material -- misreading even a single question will impact the grade you receive because of the insanely high mean.

Quiz 1 was a replica of the sample quiz the professor provided, Quiz 2 was almost the same as the sample but with a few questions he answered in class (so stop skipping class after Quiz 1), and finals was more difficult and placed greater emphasis on testing your logical thinking and understanding of the course beyond the slides.

Assessment Weights:
10% Homework
10% Participation (6% for reciting 6 times, 4% for not disturbing class)
45% Quizzes 1,2
35% Finals

Exam Statistics:
Quiz 1 – Mean of 20.3/22, SD of 3.2
Quiz 2 – Mean of 17.4/23, SD of 4.7
Final – Mean of 25.1/35, SD of 5.9

I received 21/22 for Quiz 1, 21/23 for Quiz 2, and 26/35 for Finals; participation was perfect and lost a few marks in homework, but still above mean. I think the mean of the final grade for the course is around 78% and I received 84.1%. That was a B.
sections.workload:
Workload is very light. Just three assignments with about 5 to 6 questions each; professor gives a MCQ sample midterm/final and asks you to logically show how you arrived at your answer for some questions. He also provides the answer key to the samples, so no problem.

No other BS like constructing spreadsheets was covered. Other professors had groupworks to construct an Excel sheet as assignments. But then, Excel is a pretty good skill, so if you want to learn, take the class of another professor.

If you generally do well in exams, and can ensure that careless mistakes will be minimised, definitely take this class. However, for most other people, you will likely beat yourself up for getting a mistake in a question. There’s also the tendency to feel that your efforts aren’t rewarded due to the disproportion of the insanely high mean and your level of understanding/effort that you invested to revise the powerpoint.

sections.content: Basic prob and stat, sampling, confidence interval, hypothesis testing, simple regression. Emphasis is put on how to use the formulas (plugging the numbers in), not rigorous mathematical proofs (which is a nightmare for many people, I suppose). Students with strong prob and stat background (e.g. took HKDSE M1 or stat-related subjects in high school) generally have an advantage here. But I took M2 instead of M1, and was perfectly fine with the teaching.
sections.teaching:

Tips: Don't try to skip classes unless u are a genius. Prof's notes are too simplified for understanding the course content, but is good for following his teaching in class and for revision. Studying the textbook before every lesson can help u follow the in-class teaching. Also prof will tell u what the main focus of the quizzes and finals will be (e.g. types of questions that definitely won't appear) so it's good to go to classes.
Had 2 tutorials, before assignments 1 and 2 respectively to help with Excel techniques related to data handling. Not necessary if u are already very familiar with Excel, but highly recommended if u aren't.
Prof has a bit of his own accent, but easy to follow once u get used to it.

sections.content:
Very good content. I once thought that statistic was just about playing with numbers and nothing else, while in this course I learned how powerful statistics is in representing real-life data and its power in forecasting.

Syllabus:
- Data and variation.
- Time series data.
- Transform data.
- Probability and its rules.
- Tools for organizing probability.
- Probability models.
- Variance and volatility of investments.
- Association and dependence.
- Covariance and portfolio.
- Normal probability distribution.
- Sampling.
- Sampling distributions.
- Standard errors and confidence intervals.
- Statistical hypothesis testing.
- Fitting equation to data.
- The simple regression model. ( Everything learned before is preparing you to delve into this course's most important part!! Regression is used to do forecasting!)
- Inference about SRM
- Introduction to multiple regression.
sections.teaching: Professor Hu teaches experientially, using real-life cases and experiments to demonstrate the statistics concepts. Contrary to the mathematical way of teaching, this method vividly illustrated that there were stories behind the seemingly lifeless numbers. I learned to really appreciate the beauty and the power of the statistical tools mentioned.
sections.grading:
My grade: A+

Attendance: 5%
Assignment: 15%
Exams: 80%

2 group assignments.

The format of midterm1,2 and final will be all multiple choices.

There are two weighted methods for midterms and the final exam, and whichever favors me more will be my score.
Method 1: midterm1*20%+midterm2*20%+final*40%
Method 2: midterm1*5%+midterm2*25%+final*50%
So if I screwed up my midterm1, I can still double it down on my mid2 and final to rescue my grade.

Final: 41/44, ( mean: 29, sd: 6.14)( main coverage: Regression)

All the midterms and final are non-cumulative but bear in mind that previous knowledge is a prerequisite for understanding subsequent content, so even if they are not tested, you have to know the prior content very well in order to beat the final boss: Regression.

sections.content:
The content in this course is not that hard. I personally found it quite interesting as it explains how statistics are utilised in business.
The syllabus is as follows:
Topic 1- Data description
- Recognizing the type of data
- Using graphs to see the characteristics of data
- Summarizing messy data into neat numbers
Topic 2- Probability
- Probability
- Random variable, distribution
- Discrete random variables: binomial distribution
- Continuous random variables: normal distribution, t distribution
Topic 3- Estimation
- Point estimate
- Sampling distribution
- confidence intervals
Topic 4- Hypothesis testing
- One sample, statistically significant? Using t-test
- Errors of statistical testing: Type I and Type II error

- Examining relationships for nominal and ordinal data – Chi-square test
Topic 5- Simple Linear regression
- Basic concept
- Checking model assumption
- Testing beta
- Prediction and Estimation
sections.teaching:
1. Her teaching is above average. She reads out from the slides and tends to support them with examples.
2. There is no attendance
3. Attend the classes before the quiz and exam as she tells you what will be tested. Don't depend on your classmates to tell you that.
4. She holds office hours to answer your questions.
5. TA, Elvis is one the least helpful guy you will find. Don't depend on him for anything. He barely answers e-mails. He probably should be a student to learn the course first.
sections.grading:
Grading for the course is quite fair.
There are two quizzes and a final. The tested content is non-cumulative. However, you need an understanding of the previous chapters to score high in the final. Quizzes are fairly easy and the final is easy as well. (One A4 handwritten cheatsheet is allowed.)
10% is homework and another 10% is for class participation. For participation, you need participation cards to get a full grade. If you are unable to, then games are conducted by the TA, where you can earn these points.
Your grade in the course is based on:
Quiz 1 10%
Quiz 2 20%
Final Exam 50%
Homework 10%
Performance through the Curriculum 10%
Total of 100%
Lab sessions are also there but they are not mandatory. It was tested only in the first quiz. Timings are given on canvas.
I have attached the course outline below.

sections.content:
An introductory statistics course which fits into the ISOM department. Basically DSE M1 (or IB Maths HL topic 7 (option) - probability and statistics) or equivalent.

Course Structure:

Part 1: Data and Variation
Variance, correlation, standard deviation......
This part is a recap of what you've learnt in secondary school. You will understand this if you could enter HKUST.

Part 2: Probability
Basic probability, joint, and conditional probability, random variables, covariance, normal quantile plot.....
An extension of part 1, but still quite easy and at this part of the course you can still chill and skip some lessons.

Part 3: Inference
sampling, confidence interval, hypothesis testing.....
This part requires some deeper understanding about statistics. If you have not studied M1 in secondary school, attend all lectures and ask the professor when you don't understand. Part 3 is the most important part, as part 4 is built on the basics of part 3.

Part 4: Linear Regression
residual plot, prediction interval, variation, time series....
This part requires some revision and full focus in lectures. If you skip lectures, you might get lost in the content. This part new to most students as it is not in the DSE M1 AND IB Maths HL syllabus.
sections.teaching:
The professor is very nice as he will patiently answer all questions after class. He also jokes around sometimes and this makes him a very friendly and fun professor. He even took a photo with me after the final lesson I'm very touched! He recognizes me outside the lesson. Very friendly professor and very easy to approach.

Despite many complaints about his accent, it is easy to get used to after a few lectures. It is not a problem at all after 3-4 lectures.

Interactive teaching as he encourages in-class participation and there are 2 in-class games, which is pretty fun. Rumors say the games are a part of attendance but that was never made clear by neither the professor nor the TA.
sections.grading:
Assignments 10%
Quizzes 45% (quiz 1 22% + quiz 2 23%)
Final exam 35%
Participation 10% (6% for getting parti cards from answering questions in class + 4% for not undermining class environment)

Grading is fair. However the mean is quite high as part 1-3 in the syllabus is relatively easy. Here are some stats of the exams provided by the TA:
Quiz 1 (Out of 23 marks):
Mean: 20.80   SD: 2.21
Quiz 2 (Out of 22 marks):
Mean: 18.56   SD: 2.32
Final exam (Out of 35 marks):
Mean: 28.74   SD: 3.627

As you can observe in the stats, the mean dropped significantly in the finals. Part 4 is quite challenging and requires more revision. Therefore part 4 should be the spotlight of your revision, and it somehow decides if you will get an A, B or C.

Personally, I got 89.x% (missed 0.x% in homework D:) and got a B. The grade cutoff of A range is 95%. The grade is only fair under a curved grading system.
sections.workload:
SUPER LIGHT WORKLOAD. There are only 3 assignments throughout the whole course, which takes under an hour to finish each of them (even if you don't know how to do the homework it won't take over 3 hours). The length of each assignment is quite short. It is about showing steps and reasoning in finding the answers of the MCs in the practice quizzes/final.

There are practice quizzes/final before each exam. But those are not compulsory to do so it doesn't count as high workload. Each practice quiz/final is exactly as long as an exam paper, so it doesn't take long to finish one also.

Personally, I think the biggest workload in the course is copying cheat sheets before each exam. Cheat sheet is allowed, so everyone will try their best to copy everything in the syllabus down. Some even copy the whole practice quiz/final down on the cheet sheet LOL! (including yours truly).

Overall light workload.

sections.content:
The content is very interesting and easy to understand.  It is definitely one of the best business foundation courses that what a UNIVERSITY-level course should be.  The reason why some people think that the content is complicated and hard might probably be that they compare this course to secondary school stuff.

Two huge problems of this course are no Python and too few mathematical formulae, concepts and proofs.  These are the critical elements of what a statistical course should be.  Without these, students can only learn from the tip of an iceberg.

Description Statistics and Central Tendency, Normal Distribution, PDF CDF, Population and Sample, Central Limit Theorem, Confidence Interval, Hypothesis Testing, Linear Regression Model, ...  Simply the basics
sections.teaching:
He used to teach Python but this is the first semester that he changed to teach Excel.  In fact, Python is much more useful than Excel, and therefore should be a programming language that everyone should learn.  I strongly recommend and encourage Prof. Wan to teach Python again.

Also, it can be seen that he put a lot of effort into making his powerpoints great.  The concepts are explained very clearly, even though mostly graphics.  The animations help us understand as well.  The powerpoints include all the brief yet important key points necessary for exams.  Although the explanations are not in the powerpoint, they are taught in the lectures, so make sure not to skip lessons.  To be honest, no further resources such as e-books or online learning platform videos are needed unless students skip classes very often.
sections.grading:
A. Participation (15%): In-class surveys using Canvas App will be given to get instant feedback from students.  Meanwhile, students feedback will be counted as participation.  No actual attendance is counted since email notification will be given.  Also, no correct answer is needed, simply type something to get a full mark, credited on submission.

B. Two projects (20%): Students are allowed to work individually or in groups (group size ≤ 4).  Just start doing the night before the deadline.  Everyone gets almost full marks.

C. Midterm (30%): In-class midterm.  14 MCQs.  One A4 two-sided cheat sheet allowed.  Again, everyone gets almost full marks, so it's all about carefulness.

D. Final (35%): In principle, the final will test contents discussed after the midterm, except some basic statistical concepts.  41 MCQs.  One A4 two-sided cheat sheet allowed.  Even easier than the midterm, but some questions are a bit tricky.
sections.workload: Almost no workload, just two mini-projects, two exams, and some participation.  A simple cheat sheet and a basic understanding of statistics will do.

sections.content:
This is the first semester he switched from python to microsoft excel (finally). The course itself is based on a textbook and before the lesson begins, he assigns some pre-reading. But the order of teaching is unscrambled and if you have an e-book, you'll scroll a lot to find the chapter. (I'm not joking)
He makes powerpoints on his own including different animations in an attempt to explain the statistical concepts but frankly speaking, even if you paid attention in the lesson, you forget what the animations were about quite easily.
You will do a lot of in-class exercises using excel but at least in terms of excel, it's quite straightforward.
From section 3.3 onwards, the level of difficulty suddenly jumps and concepts are really hard to comprehend. (loads of formulas and etc.)
sections.teaching:
Unless you have someone else to explain the concepts to you, it's really hard to follow. His explanation is really vague and even if you ask questions later - although it seems like he tries his best to answer to your questions - it's not much different. If you speak in Mandarin though, it seems like you can get better answers for your questions.
He often tries to interact with students by asking questions but if your session is full of quiet and shy people, it could be real uncomfortable to stay in the lecture.
In terms of Excel, he often shows his lack of understanding on how to use Excel.
In a nutshell, I think it's more or less a self taught subject and don't expect much from both TA and the professor himself.
sections.grading:
A. Participation (15%): In-class surveys using canvas App. This is more or less an attendance grade since he does it every class.  
B. Two projects (20% ): Again, you need a person who knows statistics well. It could be real pain if none of your group mate knows how to work on it. Projects are not easy at all either.
C. Midterm(30%): In-class midterm. Relatively easier but average is obviously mad high (12/14) since it's UST.
D. Final(35%): Noncumulative (thank god) BUT the level of difficulty jumps by 10000 feet from the midterm and even the prof is aware of this... Mean and median are roughly 50%. Some questions were badly sentenced that they were difficult to understand.

And the grading is very harsh as well. If you get over 80%, you can get a B. If you have any component that is below the mean, you can easily fall to a C-range.
sections.workload: Workload doesn't seem to be much apart from Project II because of its difficulty. However, if you are a keen reader and would love to do all the assigned pre-readings before the lecture, the workload will get a lot heavier because sometimes, he assigns one whole chapter as a pre-reading material.

sections.content:
Brief introduction to business statistics

Objective of the course is to equip you with basic concepts and methods of statistics  so that they can handle uncertainty intelligently in business environment.
These concepts/methods include descriptive statistics, probability, statistical inference, and linear regression.

The course adopts the following approaches to meet the objectives :
Hand-on experiences on data collection and analysis through in-class experiments
Connection to real life and business practice through thecontent of lectures
Emphasize concepts understanding  & results interpretation over procedure execution & computation throughmethods of assessment

sections.content:
Covers the following areas:

1. Descriptive Statistics
2. Probability
3. Random Variables (Discrete Random and Continuous Random)
4. Estimation (Sampling distribution and confidence intervals)
5. Hypothesis testing
6. Simple Linear Regression

The content is actually quite useful from a business pov, although I think it's really boring. The first few topics are easier but from estimation, HT and SLR, the level of difficulty shot up exponentially lol

Anyway, I heard other ISOM2500 classes had to learn multiple linear regression and get it tested during finals. So PAN's class is already quite nice for only requiring simple linear regression only.

There are 4 lab sessions. The TA will teach you how to use data analysing softwares. (p.s. some lab ppt content appeared in quiz 1)
sections.teaching:
PAN is one of the best teachers in HKUST. She is extremely nice and kind, and usually a lot of students ask her questions after class. She answers all questions one by one patiently. She even organised extra Q&A sessions (4 in total) before finals.

Her powerpoints are probably one of the best and clearest ISOM2500 ppts, and her examples are very good too. Her teaching is clear and she likes using analogies to make things simpler and easier to understand. When she notices students have difficulties following, she repeats the topic the next week.

Although there is 10% for class participation, PAN lets her students get these 10% by answering questions in class (you get a card that you submit by the end of class). She says this is because she understands some students are shy and she wants the class participation marks to be fair for both outgoing and shy students.
sections.grading:
Includes the following:
Homework (group project): 10%
Quizzes: 30%
Final: 50%
Class Participation: 10%

Most people score pretty good for homework.

Quizzes are quite difficult. Not to mention finals. All quizzes and finals are MCs.

The good thing about PAN is sometimes you get cards even though you answer incorrectly (you need to explain how you got your answer though), or even when you ask a question (has to be meaningful though!)

There are also two games throughout the year to get 2% per game. So you can answer only 6 questions + attend 2 games to get full mark for participation.
sections.workload:
Workload is tough as there are 4 lab sessions and 4 group works (homework).

Lab is not quite tough as it is optional and is usually at night, so it won't clash with your course timetable most of the time.

The tough part is the group work, as the difficulty increases drastically per assignment, and if your group mates don't study or pay attention in class, you're doomed lol

But most people manage to submit homework in time and get a satisfactory score.

sections.content: Very easy compare with other professor. No need to study computer programming language. Just use simple calculation is fine.

sections.grading: Grading of this course is quite good. There were 5 assignments, 1 midterm test and a final exam.
